---
title: "Annotation Types"
---

CodeBook Lab reads annotation definitions from the CodeBook Studio `codebook.json` format and supports five annotation types. For each type, this page shows the codebook definition, what the model is asked to return, and how its answer is checked and scored.

## Checkbox

Checkbox annotations are binary yes/no judgements. Lab stores them as `1` for yes and `0` for no.

```json
{
  "name": "Explicit evaluation",
  "type": "checkbox",
  "tooltip": "Tick this if the text clearly expresses an evaluative stance."
}
```

The model is asked to respond with `1` for yes or `0` for no. Lab also accepts JSON booleans and yes/no or true/false strings. Invalid responses are retried and then stored as blank.

When scoring, a blank checkbox counts as `0`, on both the human and the model side. So a model that never gives a valid answer is scored as answering "no" every time, not as missing. Check `output.csv` for blanks if checkbox scores look suspiciously close to the share of "no" labels.

## Dropdown

Dropdown annotations require one value from a fixed option set.

```json
{
  "name": "Direction",
  "type": "dropdown",
  "options": ["positive", "negative", "mixed", "no clear sentiment"]
}
```

The model is asked to respond with one of the listed options. Lab matches its answer to the options ignoring case and surrounding spaces or backticks, so a response such as `" Positive "` is stored as `positive` if that is how the option is spelled in the codebook. Anything that isn't one of the options is invalid and retried.

## Likert

Likert annotations require a whole number inside a configured range.

```json
{
  "name": "Intensity",
  "type": "likert",
  "min_value": 1,
  "max_value": 5
}
```

The model is asked for a whole number in the range. Numeric answers are converted to whole numbers by dropping any decimals (so `3.7` becomes `3`) and then clamped to the range (so `7` on a 1–5 scale becomes `5`). If the answer isn't valid JSON but contains a number inside the range, Lab uses that number. Otherwise the answer is invalid and retried.

Likert fields are scored twice: as categories (accuracy, F1, kappa, as for dropdowns) and as ordered values (Spearman correlation and quadratic weighted kappa), so near misses can be told apart from answers at the wrong end of the scale.

## Textbox

Textbox annotations store short free-text responses.

```json
{
  "name": "Evidence",
  "type": "textbox",
  "tooltip": "Provide a short phrase from the text that supports the judgement."
}
```

The model is asked for a brief text answer. An empty answer is invalid and retried.

Textbox generation and scoring are off by default, because the similarity metrics need optional dependencies. Turn them on per run:

```python
ExperimentSpec(
    task="policy-sentiment",
    model="gemma3:270m",
    process_textbox=True,
)
```

Install `codebook-lab[textbox]` to score them (see [Installation](install.qmd#python-environment)). Answers are lowercased and trimmed before comparison. Percentage agreement counts exact matches only, so the similarity metrics are the more useful scores for free text.

## Span

Span annotations store character offsets into the original text. They can be unlabelled highlights or labelled spans.

Unlabelled span:

```json
{
  "name": "Evidence",
  "type": "span",
  "tooltip": "Highlight the phrase that supports your judgement.",
  "label_options": []
}
```

Labelled span:

```json
{
  "name": "Emotion markers",
  "type": "span",
  "tooltip": "Tag each highlight with the emotion it conveys.",
  "label_options": ["joy", "sadness", "anger", "fear", "surprise", "disgust"]
}
```

The model is asked for a JSON list of `{"start", "end", "text"}` objects (plus `"label"` for labelled spans), using 0-indexed character offsets into the text, or `[]` if nothing applies.

Span generation and scoring are off by default. Turn them on per run:

```python
ExperimentSpec(
    task="discrete-emotions",
    model="gemma3:270m",
    process_span=True,
)
```

Span cells are CSV-safe JSON strings:

```json
[
  {"start": 38, "end": 55, "text": "her heart pounded", "label": "fear"}
]
```

Lab validates the offsets and drops spans that fall outside the text or end before they start. It then fills each span's `text` from the source using the offsets, so the stored text always matches the offsets even if the model quoted something else. Labels that are not in `label_options` are removed, leaving an unlabelled span.

An empty list (`[]`, "nothing to highlight") is stored as a blank cell, the same as an answer that could not be parsed at all. The difference only shows up in the run's logs: an unparseable answer is retried, an empty list is not.

## Built-In Example Coverage

The bundled `policy-sentiment` task exercises checkbox, dropdown, Likert, and textbox annotations. The bundled `discrete-emotions` task exercises dropdown, Likert, unlabelled span, and labelled span annotations.
